question: Which statement about the Cook–Levin theorem and NP-completeness is correct?
options: The Cook–Levin theorem shows that Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete: SAT is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time, while whether SAT itself has a polynomial-time algorithm remains open.
The Cook–Levin theorem proves P = NP, because reducing every NP problem to SAT in polynomial time gives a polynomial-time algorithm for each NP problem.
Richard Karp, not Cook, first proved that Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete in 1972; Cook's 1971 paper only defined the class NP.
Because every NP problem reduces to SAT in polynomial time, finding a polynomial-time algorithm for SAT would not settle the P versus NP question.
gold_answer: The Cook–Levin theorem shows that Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete: SAT is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time, while whether SAT itself has a polynomial-time algorithm remains open.
notes: All quoted passages come from the two linked Wikipedia articles, read live on 2026-11-19. Re-check the quoted sentences against the live pages before freezing.

positions.answer: The Cook–Levin theorem proves P = NP, because reducing every NP problem to SAT in polynomial time gives a polynomial-time algorithm for each NP problem.

claims.text: The Cook–Levin theorem establishes that P equals NP.

evidence.text: An important consequence of this theorem is that if there exists a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for solving Boolean satisfiability, then every NP problem can be solved by a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The question of whether such an algorithm for Boolean satisfiability exists is thus equivalent to the P versus NP problem, which is still widely considered the most important unsolved problem in theoretical computer science.

Although a solution to an NP-complete problem can be verified "quickly", there is no known way to find a solution quickly. That is, the time required to solve the problem using any currently known algorithm increases rapidly as the size of the problem grows.

claims.verdict_rationale: Both passages describe the P versus NP question as unsolved and say no quick way to find solutions is known; a theorem that established P = NP could not leave the question open.

claims.text: There is a known deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for Boolean satisfiability.

evidence.text: Although many practical instances of SAT can be solved by heuristic methods, the question of whether there is a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for SAT (and consequently all other NP-complete problems) is still a famous unsolved problem, despite decades of intense effort by complexity theorists, mathematical logicians, and others.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage explicitly states that whether SAT has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is still an unsolved problem, which refutes the claim that such an algorithm is known.

claims.text: The Cook–Levin theorem shows that Boolean satisfiability can be decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.

evidence.text: A decision problem is in NP if it can be decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.

The Cook–Levin theorem states that the Boolean satisfiability problem is NP-complete, establishing for the first time that such problems do exist.

claims.text: Karp proved 3SAT NP-complete by reducing SAT to 3SAT in polynomial time.

evidence.text: Karp showed each of his problems to be NP-complete by reducing another problem (already shown to be NP-complete) to that problem. For example, he showed the problem 3SAT (the Boolean satisfiability problem for expressions in conjunctive normal form (CNF) with exactly three variables or negations of variables per clause) to be NP-complete by showing how to reduce (in polynomial time) any instance of SAT to an equivalent instance of 3SAT.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states exactly that Karp showed 3SAT NP-complete by a polynomial-time reduction from SAT.
